  • Just ask: a polite, well-timed request after delivery is compliant and effective — many happy buyers simply forget until asked.
  • Use official programs: where a marketplace offers a sanctioned review program, use it rather than back channels.
  • Make the product and experience great: genuinely good products and smooth service generate reviews naturally.

Handle negative reviews well

A few negatives are normal and even build credibility — an all-perfect profile looks suspicious. Respond professionally, fix the underlying issue, and use the feedback. A well-handled complaint can win more trust than a flawless record.

Play the long game

Genuine reviews accumulate steadily and compound with your product quality and support. It is slower than buying them, but it is the only version that lasts — and it keeps your account safe.

title: A/B testing your store without fooling yourself
metaDescription: A/B testing finds what actually lifts conversion — if you do it correctly. Here is how to test properly and avoid the common traps.
bodyHtml:
A/B testing — showing two versions of a page to different visitors and seeing which performs better — is how you improve a store with evidence instead of opinion. Done badly, though, it produces confident-sounding conclusions that are simply wrong. Here is how to test properly.

Test one meaningful thing at a time

Change one element — a headline, an image, a button, a layout — so you know what caused any difference. Testing several changes at once tells you something moved but not what. And test things that could actually matter; tiny tweaks rarely move the needle enough to notice.

Respect the numbers

  • Enough traffic and conversions: small samples produce random results that look real. Low-traffic stores often cannot test reliably — that is fine, focus on bigger fixes instead.
  • Let it run long enough: ending a test the moment it looks good is how you fool yourself.
  • Do not peek and stop early at the first favourable swing.

Start with high-impact pages

Test where the traffic and the money are — your key product pages, category pages and checkout. A win on a high-traffic product page is worth more than a win on a page few people see.

Build a habit, not a one-off

The value comes from a steady stream of tests, each building on the last. Keep a simple record of what you tried and learned. If your store lacks the traffic to test reliably, prioritise the proven fundamentals first — speed, clarity, trust — and revisit testing as you grow.

title: Product photography that sells online
metaDescription: Images do most of the selling online. Here is how to get product photography that lifts conversion and cuts returns, on any budget.
bodyHtml:
Online, buyers cannot touch your product — so your photos do the selling. Weak images undercut even a great product, while strong ones lift conversion and cut returns because buyers know what they are getting. The good news: you do not need a huge budget to get this right.

The shots every product needs

  • A clean main image: the product clear and well-lit on a plain background, filling the frame.
  • Multiple angles: so buyers can see it properly.
  • Detail shots: texture, materials, finish, key features.
  • Scale reference: show size in a real context so buyers are not surprised.
  • Lifestyle images: the product in use, which helps buyers imagine owning it.

Quality basics that matter most

Good, even lighting and sharp focus do more than expensive gear. Consistent style across your catalogue looks professional and builds trust. Many strong catalogues are shot with a modest camera or a good phone and careful lighting — technique beats equipment.

Photos reduce returns

A big share of returns come from products not matching expectations. Honest, detailed images — accurate colour, true scale, real texture — set correct expectations and cut those returns, which ties straight into reducing return rates.

Meet each channel's standards

Marketplaces have image rules, and fashion channels like Myntra expect model shots. Shoot to the highest standard you need and reuse across channels. If you would like production support, our team can help brief and manage it.

title: Bundling and cross-selling to lift average order value
metaDescription: Getting each customer to spend a little more is one of the cheapest ways to grow. Here is how to use bundles and cross-sells well.
bodyHtml:
You have already paid to win the customer and get them to checkout — so getting each order a little larger is one of the cheapest forms of growth there is. Bundling and cross-selling do exactly that, when done with the buyer's interest in mind rather than as a pushy add-on. Here is how.

Bundling: sell the complete solution

Group products that naturally go together and offer them as a bundle, ideally at a small saving versus buying separately. It works because it is genuinely convenient — the buyer gets the whole solution in one go — and it raises order value while moving more units. The best bundles solve a need, not just pad the cart.

Cross-selling and upselling

  • Cross-sell: suggest relevant complementary products — the accessory for the device, the refill for the product.
  • Upsell: offer a better or larger version where it genuinely serves the buyer.

Relevance is everything — irrelevant suggestions just add clutter and erode trust.

Where to place them

Product pages (frequently-bought-together), the cart, and post-purchase flows are all natural spots. Keep it helpful and unobtrusive; the aim is to assist the buyer, not to nag. A good suggestion feels like service, a bad one feels like a sales pitch.

Measure average order value

Track AOV and watch how bundles and cross-sells move it, without hurting conversion or driving returns. Lifting AOV even modestly improves your acquisition economics across the board. Our development team can build these merchandising features into your store.

title: Planning your annual e-commerce calendar
metaDescription: The brands that win the big sales periods planned months ahead. Here is how to build an annual calendar so nothing catches you off guard.
bodyHtml:
The difference between brands that thrive during big sales periods and those that scramble usually comes down to one thing: a calendar. When you plan the year ahead, inventory, campaigns and cash are ready when the demand arrives instead of after. Here is how to build one.

Map the peaks first

Mark the major events that matter for your category — the big festive sale periods, seasonal peaks, and any dates specific to your products. In India that means the festive run and marketplace events like the big billion-day and great-festival sales, covered in our festive-season prep guide. These are the tentpoles the rest of the plan hangs on.

Work backwards from each peak

  • Inventory: order early enough to arrive and clear inbound before the rush.
  • Cash: fund that stock in advance — see managing cashflow.
  • Campaigns: plan and warm up ads before the event, not on day one.
  • Listings and site: refresh and stress-test ahead of the traffic spike.

Fill the quiet periods too

Do not only plan around peaks. Use slower months to launch products, build content and SEO, gather reviews, and run smaller promotions so momentum never fully stalls. A steady baseline makes the peaks bigger.

Keep it living

Review the calendar each month, learn from what worked, and adjust. A plan you revisit beats a plan you file away. Our marketplace management team builds and runs this calendar with clients so the whole year is deliberate, not reactive.

title: Choosing the right marketplace mix for your brand
metaDescription: You do not have to sell everywhere. Here is how to choose the marketplaces that fit your product, margins and capacity — and ignore the rest.
bodyHtml:
It is tempting to list everywhere at once, but spreading thin across a dozen marketplaces usually means doing all of them badly. The brands that win pick a focused mix that fits their product, margins and capacity. Here is how to choose yours.

Start with where your buyers are

Different marketplaces serve different shoppers. General marketplaces like Amazon and Flipkart reach broad audiences; fashion lives on Myntra; value-led volume on Meesho; everyday essentials on quick commerce. Match channels to where your specific customer actually shops.

Weigh each channel honestly

  • Margin fit: can your product make money there after all fees?
  • Competition: can you realistically stand out in that category?
  • Operational load: each channel needs listings, inventory sync, support and ads — do you have the capacity to run it well?

Depth beats breadth

Two or three marketplaces run well will out-earn six run poorly. Each channel rewards attention — good listings, stock, reviews and ads — and neglected channels drag on your metrics and your time. Prove and optimise one, then add the next.

Do not forget your own store

Marketplaces bring reach; your own store brings margin and the customer relationship — the trade-off in marketplaces vs your own store. The strongest mix usually combines a focused set of marketplaces with a D2C store. Our marketplace team helps brands pick and run the mix that actually fits them.
